title: Food & drink
goal: Name everyday Gujarati foods, say what you want and what you like, describe tastes and order at a restaurant.
intro:
Gujarati food is famously vegetarian, slightly sweet, and served as a **થાળી** *thāḷī*: dal, rice, rotli, vegetables, kadhi and sweets on one plate. Gujaratis say **જમવું** *jamvuṃ* for 'to have a meal' and **ખાવું** *khāvuṃ* for 'to eat' in general.

The key grammar here is the **dative subject**: 'I like' is literally 'to me it pleases' — મને ગમે છે.

f · મને ભૂખ લાગી છે 'I'm hungry'
f · મને તરસ લાગી છે 'I'm thirsty'
f · usually milky, sweet, with ginger or masala
f · drunk with almost every lunch
f · thick millet bread: રોટલો roṭlo (m)
m · Gujarati snacks: ઢોકળાં, ખાખરા, થેપલાં, ફાફડા

phrases.native: મને ગુજરાતી ખાવાનું બહુ ગમે છે.
phrases.roman: mane gujarātī khāvānuṃ bahu game chhe.

phrases.en: Could you bring a few more rotlis?

grammar.title: 'I like': મને … ગમે છે
grammar.body:
To say you like something, Gujarati makes the **person who likes** dative (with -ને) and the **thing liked** the subject: **મને ચા ગમે છે** 'I like tea' (lit. 'to me tea is pleasing').

Dative pronouns: મને 'to me', તને 'to you (intimate)', તમને 'to you (polite)', એને 'to him/her', અમને / આપણને 'to us', એમને 'to them / him (respectful)'. With nouns, add -ને: સીતાને 'to Sita'.

Negative: **મને … નથી ગમતું** (the verb takes the -તું form and agrees with the thing: ગમતો m, ગમતી f, ગમતું n).

examples.native: મારા ભાઈને ઢોકળાં બહુ ગમે છે.
examples.roman: mārā bhāīne ḍhokḷāṃ bahu game chhe.

grammar.title: 'I want / need': મને … જોઈએ છે
grammar.body:
**જોઈએ** *joīe* works the same way: the person is dative, the thing wanted is the subject. **મને ચા જોઈએ છે** 'I want tea'. In shops and restaurants the છે is often dropped: **મને બે સમોસા જોઈએ** 'I'd like two samosas'.

Negative: **મને નથી જોઈતું** (agrees: જોઈતો / જોઈતી / જોઈતું) or simply **નથી જોઈતું, આભાર** 'I don't need it, thanks'.

Hunger and thirst also use the dative with **લાગવું** 'to strike, be felt': મને ભૂખ લાગી છે 'hunger has struck me'.

examples.native: મને એક ગ્લાસ પાણી જોઈએ છે.
examples.roman: mane ek glās pāṇī joīe chhe.
examples.en: I want a glass of water.
How many rotlis do you want?

dialogue.title: Lunch at a thali restaurant
dialogue.setting: Ravi and his friend Ella sit down at a busy thali restaurant in Ahmedabad.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: હા, બે થાળી. અને બે છાશ પણ.
lines.roman: hā, be thāḷī. ane be chhāsh paṇ.
lines.en: Yes, two thalis. And two buttermilks too.

lines.speaker: Ella
lines.native: રવિ, આ શું છે? બહુ ગળ્યું છે!
lines.roman: Ravi, ā shuṃ chhe? bahu gaḷyuṃ chhe!
lines.en: Ravi, what's this? It's very sweet!

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: એ ગુજરાતી દાળ છે. તને ગમે છે?
lines.roman: e gujarātī dāḷ chhe. tane game chhe?
lines.en: That's Gujarati dal. Do you like it?

lines.speaker: Ella
lines.native: હા, બહુ સ્વાદિષ્ટ છે. પણ આ શાક થોડું તીખું છે.
lines.roman: hā, bahu svādiṣṭ chhe. paṇ ā shāk thoḍuṃ tīkhuṃ chhe.
lines.en: Yes, it's delicious. But this vegetable is a bit spicy.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: Madam, shall I give you a rotli?

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.en: A little rice? A little kadhi?

culture: In a Gujarati home or thali restaurant, servers keep refilling your plate until you firmly say **બસ** *bas* 'enough' — and even then a host may insist (આગ્રહ *āgrah*). Leaving a little food signals you are full. Many Gujaratis are strict vegetarians, and Jains avoid root vegetables such as onion, garlic and potato; ask **જૈન છે?** if you're unsure.
